title: CMPC scope compared with other professionals
body: A CMPC teaches and applies mental performance skills such as focus, confidence, arousal regulation, goal setting, and team dynamics. Many neighboring jobs overlap with that work, so scope questions arise naturally. Licensed clinicians (such as psychologists, counselors, social workers, psychiatrists) diagnose and treat mental disorders as their licenses allow; a CMPC without such a license does not. Athletic trainers, physicians, and physical therapists evaluate and treat injuries, and the designated medical authority (often the team physician) decides return to play. Strength and conditioning coaches design physical training. Registered dietitians write individualized nutrition plans and provide medical nutrition therapy. Executive coaches work on leadership and organizational issues under a title anyone can use. The working rule: a CMPC may share general, evidence-based information in these areas, but leaves assessment, diagnosis, and prescription to the right professional, and coordinates with them (with the client's consent) as part of a team.
points: Mental disorder diagnosis and treatment: licensed clinicians
Injury care and return-to-play clearance: medical team
Training programs: strength coach; meal plans: registered dietitian
General education is fine; individualized medical, clinical, nutrition, or training assessment or prescription is not
examNote: A likely scenario offers a tempting option where the consultant does another professional's job (clears an athlete to play, writes a meal plan, treats a disorder). Choose the option that stays in scope while still helping, usually by sharing general information and coordinating or referring.

title: SafeSport Code and MAAPP essentials
body: In the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, the U.S. Center for SafeSport has authority over sexual misconduct reports, may take other abuse cases, and sets abuse-prevention rules. Adults in the movement must report suspected child abuse, including sexual abuse, to law enforcement or child protective services as the law requires, and to the Center. Reporting requires reasonable suspicion, not proof. The adult who hears a disclosure should listen calmly, avoid promising secrecy, attend to safety, and report promptly. They should not investigate, gather evidence, or confront the alleged perpetrator. The Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies (MAAPP) limit risky situations: one-on-one interactions with minors must be observable and interruptible (with narrow exceptions, such as emergencies), and electronic communication with minors must be professional and transparent, for example by copying a parent or guardian. Other MAAPP areas include travel, locker rooms, and massage or athletic training modalities.
points: Report suspected abuse of a minor promptly to CPS or police, and also to the Center in Olympic/Paralympic sport
Don't investigate, confront, or promise secrecy
One-on-one with minors: observable and interruptible, in person or online
Electronic messages with minors: professional and open, e.g., parent copied
examNote: Abuse disclosures override the usual consulting sequence. The best answer reports promptly to both outside authorities and, in the Olympic movement, the Center; options that first verify the story or talk to the coach are wrong.

title: Ethical decision-making models
body: Ethical decision-making models give consultants a structured process to replace gut reaction when standards, loyalties, or stakeholders conflict. The models share a common core: recognize that an ethical issue exists; gather the facts and identify every stakeholder, including who the client is; identify the relevant Ethics Code standards, laws, and organizational policies; consult a trusted colleague or mentor while protecting identities; generate possible courses of action; weigh each option's likely consequences for everyone affected, guided by principles such as respecting autonomy, doing good, avoiding harm, fairness, and keeping commitments; choose and carry out the action; then evaluate the outcome and document the reasoning. The models don't produce automatic answers, but they make decisions more defensible and less driven by pressure, especially from people with power or money in the situation.
points: Identify the issue, the facts, and every stakeholder
Check the Code, the law, and policy; consult a colleague or mentor
Generate options and weigh consequences for each stakeholder
Act, evaluate the outcome, and document the reasoning
examNote: Expect scenarios where a consultant is pressured to act fast. Look for the option that follows the structured process, often consulting a colleague or mentor before acting, rather than deferring to the payer or acting on instinct.

title: The CMPC credential, titles, and educating consumers
body: The Certified Mental Performance Consultant (CMPC) credential from AASP shows that a practitioner has met standards for graduate education, specified coursework, mentored applied experience, and a certification exam, and keeps the credential through continuing education and recertification. It is a professional certification, not a state license. It doesn't authorize anyone to diagnose or treat mental disorders, and it doesn't make the holder a psychologist. Many jurisdictions restrict the title "psychologist" (sometimes including "sport psychologist") to licensed psychologists, so consultants must follow local law and describe themselves accurately, for example as a Certified Mental Performance Consultant with their actual degree. Educating consumers is part of the job: athletes, parents, coaches, and organizations should understand what a CMPC does, how that differs from licensed mental health care, and when a referral is appropriate.
points: CMPC = certification, never a license
Follow local law on "psychologist"; never imply licensure you lack
Explain scope clearly to clients, parents, and organizations
Advertising must be accurate: no guarantees, no overstated evidence
examNote: Wrong options often call the CMPC a license, use "psychologist" without licensure, or claim the credential permits treating disorders. The best option describes the credential accurately and points to licensed care when needed.

title: Online consulting: jurisdiction, consent, identity, emergencies
body: APA's telepsychology guidelines (written for psychologists, since revised) offer useful guidance. Before technology-mediated work begins, the consultant checks the laws and regulations where both parties are located. These cover who may provide the service, which titles are allowed, and data protection; licensed professionals must also consider licensure in the client's jurisdiction. Informed consent covers the usual elements plus technology-specific ones: the risks of the platform (breaches, recording, interception), what happens if the connection fails, how and when to use messaging, response times, and the fact that remote work may not suit every concern. At the first session the consultant verifies the client's identity. At the start of each session, the consultant confirms where the client is physically located, because emergency services must be local to the client. An emergency plan includes a backup phone number, a local emergency contact, and local crisis resources, so a dropped call has a clear next step. With minors, get guardian permission plus assent and keep one-on-one sessions observable and interruptible.
points: Follow the laws where both consultant and client are located
Consent covers technology risks, disconnection, and messaging rules
Verify identity; confirm the client's location each session
Emergency plan: backup number, local contact, local crisis resources
examNote: "First step" items in virtual settings usually favor identity verification and emergency preparedness (location, local contacts, backup plan) before intake content. Emergency calls go to services where the client is, not where the consultant is.

title: Confidentiality, HIPAA basics, and secure platforms
body: The ethical duty to protect confidentiality applies to every consultant, whatever the technology. HIPAA's Privacy and Security Rules are federal regulations that apply to covered entities (health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers who conduct certain transactions electronically, such as insurance billing) and to their business associates. Whether HIPAA applies therefore depends on the practice. Those it covers need safeguards for electronic health information and business associate agreements with vendors that handle it. Either way, consultants should use secure, encrypted platforms with access controls for video, messaging, assessment, and storage, avoid ordinary email or consumer apps for sensitive content, and tell clients how their data are handled. In group or team sessions online, encryption can't stop members from sharing what they hear, so agreed norms and honest limits of confidentiality still matter.
points: HIPAA applies to covered entities and their business associates
Ethical confidentiality duties apply regardless of HIPAA
Use encrypted, access-restricted platforms; tell clients how data are handled
Technology can't guarantee group members' discretion
examNote: Distractors claim HIPAA applies to everyone, or that being outside HIPAA removes privacy duties, or that a "HIPAA compliant" label is sufficient. The best answer pairs accurate HIPAA scope with the ethical requirement for secure communication.

title: Documentation and records with technology
body: Technology changes where records live and who can reach them, but not the obligation to keep accurate records and store them securely. For remote sessions, guidelines written for psychologists offer a useful model: document the delivery mode, the client's location, who else was present, technical disruptions, and any emergency steps taken. Records belong in encrypted, password-protected systems with access limited to people the client has agreed may see them, not on a shared organizational drive open to coaches or on an unsecured personal device. Devices that hold client information need passcodes, encryption, and automatic locking. Messages, recordings, app data, and wearable data that bear on services need the same care, and recordings require informed consent covering purpose, viewers, storage, and deletion. Records should be kept for the period required by law and policy, disposed of securely, and planned for if the consultant leaves or becomes unable to practice.
points: Document modality, client location, disruptions, and emergency actions
Encrypted, access-restricted storage; secure devices
Recordings and app or wearable data need consent and protection
Follow legal and policy retention, then dispose securely
examNote: When an organization asks for open access to notes or data, the best answer explains the confidentiality conflict and works toward restricted access, rather than complying, splitting records, or dropping documentation altogether.

title: Social media and professional conduct online
body: The Ethics Code's standards on confidentiality, multiple relationships, accurate public statements, and testimonials all apply online. Accepting friend or follow requests from current clients on personal accounts can create a social relationship alongside the professional one, so consultants usually decline, explain why, and put a written social media policy into informed consent. Merely working with someone is confidential, so posting about a client (even a public win) or a photo that implies the connection requires the client's explicit consent. Public commentary should share general, evidence-based information and never speculate about whether a specific person, especially someone the consultant has never assessed, has a mental disorder. Professional accounts should be kept separate from personal ones, marketing must be accurate, and testimonials from current clients are off limits even if they consent.
points: Decline personal connections with clients; have a written social media policy
Don't identify anyone as a client online without explicit consent
Comment generally; never speculate about a specific person's mental health
Keep professional and personal accounts separate
examNote: Look for options that set a clear, explained boundary (not silent ignoring) and that protect the existence of the consulting relationship. "It's already public" is never a reason to disclose that someone is a client.
